title: Let nothing disturb thee
hookLine: a short poem found in her breviary: all things pass, God does not change, God alone suffices

lines: A SCRAP OF PAPER, KEPT CLOSE.
cards: A note folded in a wallet. A line taped inside a cabinet. A verse on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror.
Something short enough to read with a toothbrush in your mouth, and strong enough to get through a day. Teresa of Ávila had one too.
Tradition says that after she died, her sisters found it tucked in her breviary, the prayer book she carried every day. Nine lines. People still copy them out.

teach.b: In Teresa's Spanish, it begins: "Nada te turbe, nada te espante." Let nothing disturb you, nothing frighten you. The old English version begins, let nothing disturb thee.
First, the worry. Teresa did not live a quiet life: lawsuits, sickness, travel on broken roads, officials who tried to shut down her convents. These lines aren't a greeting card.
They read like what a hard-pressed woman told herself. Second, what passes. Everything passes, the next lines say.

teach.h: ALL THINGS PASS. GOD DOES NOT.
teach.b: God does not change. Your worry, your triumph, your bad week, the officials who hate you: all of it passes. Third, patience.
Then: patience obtains everything. Not quick results. The steady waiting she learned over a lifetime of prayer.
The ending is the part people carve on walls and stitch on cushions: whoever has God lacks nothing.
And the last three words in Spanish: "Sólo Dios basta." God alone is enough. That doesn't mean Teresa didn't need friends, food or sleep.
She loved her friends fiercely and wrote to them constantly. It means that underneath everything, when all of it shakes, there is a floor. For Teresa, that floor had a name.

how: Many Catholics keep Teresa's Nada te turbe on a prayer card or say it in hard moments, and the Taizé community sings it as a short, repeated chant.

games.q: you're Teresa. your convents are under attack, you're sick, and you have a long road tomorrow. what do you keep in your prayer book?
o: a list of everyone who's against you.
nine short lines: all things pass, God alone is enough.
games.why: tradition says the nine lines were found in her breviary after she died.

practice: On a scrap of paper or a sticky note, write the first line, let nothing disturb thee, or the last, God alone is enough. Hold it, think of one thing that's disturbing you right now, and read the line to it.
If you pray, pray Teresa's lines as she did; if you don't, let the words steady you.
